BULLETS FIRED AT PURSUERS.
Negro Shot at Posse Who Attempt Capture
With a bullet through his left lung John Suggs, a young farmer living in the Fifteenth district, below Americus, lies in a critical condition and may die therefrom, while Andrew Cheney, a negro farmer, who probably fired the shot, is in jail here.

Cheney surrendered himself to Sheriff Bell yesterday and asked protection, claiming that he fired upon a posse in self defense as they attempted to break down his door.

The fatal affray occurred Saturday night and Sunday morning.

From all accounts of the tragedy received here a posses of white men were trying to get possession of Cheney, who was barricaded in his house at midnight. He refused to open the door upon their demand when, he says, they attempted to break in.

At this he fired point blank and, he claims, struck John Suggs, one of the party outside.

Others think the bullets may have been fired by one of Cheney's confederates upon the outside, who had come to his assistance.

At all events Suggs is very badly wounded and may die. The negro, Cheney, as stated, has surrendered himself and asks protection. Walter Bray, another young man who had previously had a row with Cheney, is cut on the arm, but not badly.

Reports of the trouble received here yesterday are as follows.

Cheney was driving his wagon home Saturday night and, he claims, accidentally ran into Bray's buggy. A fight in the road ensued, Bray, it is said, using a rail upon Cheney while the negro plied his knife with the result stated.

The attack upon Cheney in his house, several hours later, was the result of this fight. Four or five men constituted the avenging posse, all of whom are young men we'll known in that section, where the shooting created much excitement.

This was the story as told here yesterday, although there may be other versions of the whole affair.

LIE NEARLY CAUSED LYNCHING.
Negro Girl Confessed to Forgery When Her Father's Life Was in Danger.
NEW ORLEANS, La., Aug. 18.—Vanceville, Bossier Parish, La., has just quieted down after great excitement and a narrow escape from a quadruple lynching. Whit Vance, a leading white planter in the neighborhood, received a letter threatening his life and containing vile references to Mrs. Vance and to other members of his family. The name of Peter Dozier, a negro living at Vanceville, was signed to it.

Dozier was at once arrested and with him a negro named Andrew Miller, who had the reputation of being a dangerous negro, and two other negroes who were supposed to be accomplices. Considerable excitement prevailed and it was reported that a quadruple lynching was down on the programme. Before the lynching, however, the entire aspect of the case was changed when Annie Miller, daughter of one of the men in jail in danger of lynching, confessed that she had written the letter and forged Dozier's name to it. Jealous of Dozier, who had discarded her, she decided on revenge and hit upon the idea of, writing such a threatening letter that the whites would be aroused and probably lynch the man she hated. Her revenge was complete, but she found out that it had been so successful that her own father and two other negroes, against whom she had no grudge, would likely be lynched. She weakened and confessed in an open meeting, where the entire population of the town of Vanceville and neighborhood, white and black, were present. The meeting then unanimously resolved that the Miller girl should be whipped for the trouble she had caused and she was turned over to a committee of three and the sentence carried out. Dozier and his friends were released from jail.

The new York papers bring us the details of a "race war" that is on in Brooklyn, where Dr. Newell Dwight Hillis centers, and from whence he irradiates the earth. We feel sure that he will thank us for calling his attention to the conflict which is raging far below the eyrie from which he looks out upon "the barbarism and intolerable race prejudice" of this Southern country.

A few weeks ago the white handlers for the Export Lumber Company went on strike for time-and-a-half pay for over-time work. To supply their places the company sent South and employed a gang of negro lumbermen. These latter had no sooner gone to work than the strikers began to make their lives miserable and to threaten them with deaths of divers and sundry kinds. They were arrested and pleaded that they objected to having their jobs given to "niggers"—if they had been given to white men they, the strikers, would have had no kick coming!

That plea went with the magistrate, who fined the chief thumper $2 and discharged his three assistant nigger-punchers.

As he was once so ready to receive a negro as a guest in his home and even to make up his bed after him, why should he not be equally ready to go down to the lumber yards of Brooklyn and stand substitute for the sable sons of the South who are persona non grata to the white strikers? charley-hudson-1903-08-27.A1:
WERE ARRESTED ON PEONAGE CHARGE

Three Men Tried and Held by U. S. Commissioner

CLAIM KIDNAPPED NEGRO

Affidavit Was That Charlie Hutson Was Caught In a Public Highway and Placed in Involuntary Servitude.
CLAIM KIDNAPPED NEGRO
Marcellus Lockhart, Aaron Dill, and Archie Dill were arrested near Guin in Marion county yesterday by United States Deputy Marshal Ashley on the charge of peonage and when brought Lefore Commissioner A. C. Birch were placed in the county jail on default of $2000 bond.

The cases are set for hearing on Friday morning at 9 o'clock.

The cases were worked up by Secret Service Agent J. M. Wright, and it is said that the testimony will be the most sensational heard in the court for many a day. Peonage in Alabama has gained national notoriety during the past few months, and the announcement that examples of it have been brought to light in Marion county will command unusual attention.

Sensational Features.

The name of the negro who it is alleged was held in involuntary servitude without due sentence or conviction for crime is Charley Hutson. According to the affidavit he was unlawfully arrested, kidnapped, seized or carried away from the highway on the 27th of last August, and was forced to perform labor without pay.

Secret Service Agent Wright made a deposition before Commissioner Birch, who was only recently appointed by Judge Jones, in which he charged that on the 27th day of August, 1903, Aaron Dill, Archie Dill and Marcellus Lockhart, in Marion county, did arrest, return or caused to be held, arrested or returned, or aided in the arrest or return of one Charley Hutson, to a condition of peonage or involuntary servitude, contrary to the form of the statute in such cases made and provided against the peace and dignity of the United States.

There are two specific charges against each of the defendants, of which the peonage is one. The other is conspiracy to deprive a citizen of certain rights granted him by the constitution of the United States.

Conspiracy Charge.

In the conspiracy charge Secret Service Agent Wright also made affidavit that on the 27th day of August, 1903, the defendants did conspire to injure, oppress, threaten and intimidate one Charley Hutson, who is a citizen of the United States, in the free exercise and enjoyment of a right or privilege secured to him by the constitution or laws of the United States, to-wit, the right of liberty and exemption from imprisonment, involuntary servitude or bondage except in punishment for crime and without any crime on his part or by him committed, or conviction or sentence therefor legally had against the said Charley Hutson; and that said defendants in furtherance and execution of the said conspiracy informed and for the purposes aforesaid, and to effect the object thereof, the defendants at the time and place aforesaid forcibly and unlawfully arrested, kidnapped, seized or carried away the said Charley Hutson to render service and labor to the defendants, or one or more of them, without compensation to the said Charley Hutson, and did hold the said Charley Hutson in involuntary servitude, contrary to the form of the statute in such case made and provided and against the peace and dignity of the United States.

The affidavits were approved by Assistant United States District Attorney N. L. Steele.

A large number of witnessed will be subpoenaed in the case and it promises to attract attention throughout the whole state.
charley-hudson-1903-08-27.A4:
Charge of Peonage and Conspiracy Sustained
BOND PLACED AT $1500 E/CH
Testimony Before United States Commissioner Birch Shows Startling State of Affairs---Negroes Imprisoned and Flogged.
The preliminary hearing of Aaron Dill and his son Archie Dill, charged with peonage and with conspiracy was held before United States Commissioner A. C. Birch yesterday and the defendants were remanded to jail to await the action of the federal grand jury in default of $1500 bond. The hearing of Marcellus Lockhart on the same charges was set for October 9, and he was also placed in jail, not being able to make the $1500 bond required.

From the evidence brought out yesterday the prosecuting attorneys feel sure that they have a very strong case against these defendants. They were arrested last week near Guin in Marion county, the double charge of peonage and of conspiracy to deprive a citizen of his liberty. Assistant District Attorneys N. L. Steele and W. H. Standifer are prosecuting the cases and the defendants were represented yesterday by J. C. Miller of Vernon and S. L. Weaver and A. Leo Oberdorfer of Birmingham.

Lee Crump, another defendant under the same charges, waived examination yesterday and his case will go before the grand jury. He is out on bail.

The Evidence.

According to the evidence Charley Hudson was riding along the road by the Dill place when he was forcibly seized by the defendants and put to work. On the stand he testified that at night he was locked up in an old cotton house and that upon one occasion when he tried to escape he was caught when about two miles down the road and brought back and given ninety lashes with a hickory stick. He said that when they stopped whipping him his shirt was wet with the blood that had been drawn.

He said that the chief work he had to do was to cut railroad ties for Marshal Dill. Marshal Dill is the defendant who has not yet been caught. Hudson testified further that he was never paid anything for his work and that his clothing and $10 in money were confiscated by Marshal Dill for his own use.

Bob Stevenson was another negro put on the stand. He is the man who administered the whipping to Hudson at the command of Marshal Dill, the latter having a revolver pointed at him at the time. He said that Hudson was tied to a tree before the whipping was administered.

Stevenson said that he signed a contract to work for Mr. Dill for $9 a month for a year, and that Mr. Dill in turn leased him to Mr. Lockhart for $16 a month. He also said that he saw Mr. Dill wearing Charley Hudson's shoes after Charley had left.

C. A. Booker, a white farme,r testified that he knew all the defendants as well as the negroes and that he had seen Mr. Dill with Hudson's pants and shoes on after Hudson had left.

Ed Knight, a white miller, testified that he knew the defendants and the negroes and that a week ago Marshall Dill came to his mill with Charley Hudson and said: "I want to sell you this negro; I am going to Mississippi." He said that Hudson had a gash in his head and a large hole in his cheek. He asked Dill what right he had to sell the negro and received the reply that he (Dill) had the negro under contract. He said further that Dill insisted on selling him but that he would not buy him.

The Argument.

The arguments made by the attorneys for the defense during the afternoon were simply pleas for the release of the father on the ground that he was not cognizant of what was going on. They didn't deny that there had been flagrant violation of the law, but they maintained that the chief offender was Marshall Dill, the man who has not yet been caught.

On the other hand, the prosecuting attorneys made the most out of the evidence and Attorney Steele cited the definition of peonage as given by Judge Thomas G. Jones to the grand jury in Montgomery, which was as follows:

"A person who hires another and induces him to sign a contract by which he agrees during the term to be imprisoned or kept under guard, and under cover of such agreement afterwards holds the party to the performance of the contract by threats or punishment or undue influence, subduing his free will, when he desires to abandon the service is guilty of holding such a person to 'a condition of peonage.'"

At the conclusion of the arguments Commissioner Birch at first named the bond on which the defendants should be held at $3000 but the defense put up the plea of what poor men the defendants were and it was finally agreed by the prosecution that the bond be fixed at $1500 each.

Charley Hudson, a negro, is alleged to have been held an involuntary prisoner and horribly treated by his captors.

The testimony this morning tended to show that Hudson had been stopped on the public road near the Dill place in Lamar county some time ago and forced to work on the farm of Marshall Dill, chiefly cutting railroad ties; that at night he was placed in a cotton house without windows and with only one door, and that when he escaped Marshall Dill, aided by a negro, Bob Stevenson, pursued and caught him; and after tying him up to a tree whipped him with a stick until the blood came in a stream. Marshal Dill, alleged keeper of peons, alleged conspirator and alleged all round bad man, was captured near Amory, Miss., on Friday by Deputy United States Marshal J. D. MARSHALL DILL IS
SENT BACK TO JAIL

Bonds ut $4000

CHARGED WITH PEONAGE

spiracy—Bob Stevens, a Negro,
Is the Only Witness

CHARGED WITH PEONAGE
Marshall Dill, charged with peonage and conspiracy was yesterday remanded to jail in default of $2000 bond under each charge.

United States Commissioner Birch gave him a preliminary hearing yesterday morning. Bob Stevens, a negro, was the only witness placed on the stand, but the testimony of the former hearing in which Aaron Dill and Archie Dill, father and brother of Marshall were defendants, was submitted for consideration by the commissioner.

Marshall Dill was not caught until after the other two had been brought to Birmingham. According to the testimony at the former hearing, Marshal was the most guilty of the three, and the evidence brought out by the examination of Bob Stevens yesterday seemed to point to the same conclusion.

Stevens on the Stand.

Stevens was placed on the stand by Assistant United States Attorney N. L. Steele. He testified that he had signed a contract with Marshal Dill to work for him a year at $9 a month, but that he had never been paid any money. He said Charley Hudson was also kept by Mr. Dill and that when Hudson tried on one occasion to escape he and Mr. Dill went after him, and that when Charley started to run Mr. Dill snapped both barrels of his shotgun at him, but both failed to go off.

Tried to Cut White Man.

He also said that when Hudson was caught, he tried to cut Mr. Dill, but cut himself instead; that Mr. Dill then tied Hudson's hands behind him and marched him home and that when they reached home Archie Dill knocked the negro down with his fist while his hands were tied. He said they then tied Hudson to a tree and Marshal Dill, with a pointed pistol, commanded him (Stevens) to whip the other negro, which he did.

He said, further, that they had once had a picture taken in which Marshal Dill with a pistol in hand was standing between the two negroes, Charley Hudson and himself.

Defendant Waives Preliminary.

The defendant was represented by A. Leo Oberdorfer, who gave notice at the opening of the hearing that the defendant waived preliminary examination.

The three Dills are now confined in the county jail, as well as the negro, Bob Stevens. Stevens was made a defendant in the case on the same charges as the white men on account of his participation in certain of the alleged crimes, but he is being held chiefly because of his importance as a witness in the case.

A PRISONER FROM TEXAS

A. A. Hardie Charged with Peonage.

SON-IN-LAW OF J. W. PACE

Formerly a Guard in Tallapoosa County.

Pace Meets Him Here and Made His Bond—Witnesses from Lowndes County Before the Grand Jury.
SON-IN-LAW OF J.W. PACE
From distant Texas, a prisoner charged with peonage was last night brought to Montgomery, in the person of Anderson A. Hardie, son-in-law of J. W. Pace of Tallapoosa County and formerly a guard at Pace's convict camp.

Hardie's alleged crime was committed in Tallapoosa County. Specifically he is indicted for holding in peonage Joe Patterson, a negro, whose case was first exploited by The New York Post. Patterson is also one of the negroes whom Pace is said to have held in peonage.

The indictment against Hardie was one of the first to be found by the United States grand jury in session here. The Marshal's office immediately began to look for Hardie. He was located in Throckmorton County, Texas, where he has been a resident since December, when he left Tallapoosa County.

District Attorney Warren S. Reese received notice of the arrest of Hardie from William H. Atwell, District Attorney of the Northern District of Texas. The arrest was made about ten days ago and from that time until he left for Montgomery in charge of Deputy Marshals R. M. Warden and J. B. Girand, Hardie remained in jail at Abilene, Texas.

Hardie and his guards reached Montgomery at 6:30 o'clock yesterday evening. They at once proceeded to the office of the United States marshal, where before J. W. Dimmick, clerk of the United States Court Hardie made a $2,000 bond, which was signed by himself, G. R. Shaeffer, W. W. Hardie, a brother of the arrested man.

J. W. Pace met Hardie in Montgomery with a power of attorney from his bondsmen.

When seen last night Hardie, a young man about 30 years old, fair complexioned and tall, said that he had been advised that a true bill would probably be found against him and he immediately informed the marshal of the Northern District of Texas of his whereabouts.

He denied that he has violated any law in reference to peonage. He says that he moved from Tallapoosa County in December and since that time has been engaged in farming and other interests in Texas.

Pace, when a representative of The Advertiser approached Hardie, in a good natured way shook hands with the newspaper man and said: "Well, I expect I know about all the paper men now. I thought I had met 'em all, but you must be a new one."

Pace will leave today for Tallapoosa County. Hardie will remain in Montgomery until his trial.

All of the persons charged with peonage will be arraigned in the United States Court Monday, June 22, and their cases will be set for trial by Judge Thomas G. Jones.

H. C. Dickey of the United States Secret Service came back from Tallapoosa County yesterday, after issuing subpoenas to a number of witnesses in the peonage cases.

The grand jury continued its investigations yesterday of the alleged practice of peonage in Alabama. In the afternoon Duncan Palmer, a white man, and Philip Smith, a negro, of Lowndes County went before the jury to testify. Albert D. Washburn and James M. Harrison, well known citizens of Dadeville, were also before the grand jury.

No additional indictments were returned yesterday.

District Attorney Warren S. Reese is expected to return from Washington today where he was summoned for a conference concerning the peonage investigation.

NEGRO SLAVERY DOWN IN ALABAMA That Is What the State's System of Peonage Plainly Amounts To. CRUELTIES ARE FEARFUL Laws of the State Make This Sort of Treatment Possible—Witnesses Hard to Secure Against Perpetrators.
Montgomery, Ala., June 23.—Thus far authentic cases of peonage—slavery is a better word—have been found in three counties of Alabama—Tallapoosa, Coosa and Lowndes. The last named county is still under scrutiny. The sheriff is accused of maintaining peons in addition to controlling the regularly convicted county prisoners. His name is Dixon and he is one of five brothers who dominate the politics of Lowndes county. They are rough, violent men and they have succeeded in creating so much terror not only among the blacks but the whites of Lowndes county that witnesses against them are exceedingly difficult to obtain.

One negro named Dillard Freeman, whom three of the Dixons are said to have nearly killed because he left the sheriff's place at Hayneville and visited his mother seven miles away without permission, was pursued right to the entrance of the United States court house in Montgomery by the brothers. Freeman has been subpoened as a witness to appear before the federal grand jury. According to a story which the boy subsequently told to United States District Attorney Reese and his assistant, Mr. Sternfeldt, the brothers, one of them the sheriff, warned him that if he told the truth to the grand jury he would be killed upon his return to Lowndes county.

Dragged by a Rope.

The boy had been fearfully mal-treated. The Dixons pursued him to his mother's cabin on the occasion of his flight from Hayneville. They entered the cabin by force, took Freeman out of doors and in the presence of his mother beat him savagely over the head with pistols. Then a rope was tied around his neck and the other end fastened to a horse. Two of the Dixons took a position in the rear of the negro boy. In this order they proceeded back to Hayneville, a distance of seven miles. The boy had to keep his feet regardless of the speed at which the horse traveled or be strangled.

After he reached Hayneville he was mercilessly beaten with a gin strap across the bare back and legs. He does not know how many blows were struck, because he lost consciousness after the fifteenth, but there is testimony to prove that the total number was not less than 100. They were blows struck by a man six feet in height and weighing 250 pounds and they were blows, moreover that were administered with all the strength he could put into them. The only wonder is that the boy survived the punishment.

The most extraordinary feature of this case is that the victim was never legally convicted of an offense against the law. Dixon in his capacity as sheriff had plenty of prisoners for his chain gang who were legally convicted of wrong-doing, but he believed he needed peons and created them at will. Ostensibly he took the Freeman boy into his employ at an agreed rate of wages. The boy signed a contract by the terms of which he agreed that Dixon could treat him as a prisoner.

Education of a "Trusty."

The first experience which he recalls was one involving a beating administered by one of Dixon's subordinates. Dixon told him that they were educating him to be a trusty. The boy is now under the protection of the United States attorneys in Montgomery. The attempt of the Dixons to force him to perjure himself before the grand jury under threat of death would have been followed by quick punishment of the brothers by Judge Jones if proper corroborative proof of the episode could have been obtained.

Lowndes county is in the center of the black belt of Alabama, and its negro population outnumbers the whites nearly 10 to 1. The Dixons dominate its politics absolutely. Their influence, moreover, extends to state politics. This case serves to illustrates what peonage has brought upon the state.

The most shocking disclosures of the investigation thus far center in the counties of Coosa and Tallapoosa. Here peonage in its worst form has apparently thrived for at least fifteen years. Coosa county seems to have engaged largely in the business of creating peons and then selling them to the slave drivers of Tallapoosa county. The process was comparatively simple. A strange negro man or woman would appear in Rockford, the county seat, or Colcis or Goodwater, both of them towns in Coosa county. A constable would take them into custody and arraign them before a justice of the peace named London upon a trumped-up charge. They might be charged with obtaining money under false pretenses, drunkenness, disorderly conduct or of any one of the dozen offenses against the law of which they were innocent.

Girl Sold to Slavery.

The case of a girl about 16 years of age who was sold into slavery in Tallapoosa county by London illustrates how the traffic was carried on. The girl was traveling through Goodwater with an itinerant photographer. She was acting as cook for the photographer's outfit. Robert M. Franklin, a constable, placed her under arrest upon a charge of living in improper relations with her employer. He arraigned her before London, the justice of the peace. The latter found her guilty, but compromised the case with the girl by arranging to take her into his own household as a servant, agreeing to pay her $2 a month. He gave her credit to the extent of $3.40 at his store, for which he secured her acknowledgment to a debt judgment and then he sold the girl to Turner of Tallapoosa county.

ELI HILSON ASSASSINATED.
Waylaid and Murdered In His Buggy, While On His Way Home From Brookhaven.
Brookhaven.

Eli Hilson, a negro living about eight miles from Brookhaven, was assassinated within about a quarter of a mile of his home Saturday evening, while on his way home from town alone in his buggy. The bullet which killed him entered the side of his head near the ear and came out at the mouth. Death seems to have been instantaneous. The horse went on home, and his owner was found dead in the buggy on his arrival.

Coroner Geo. Lambright, Jr., visited the scene of the murder Monday, impaneled a jury and held an inquest, the verdict being that the deceased came to his death by a gunshot wound at the hands of parties unknown.

Last winter Hilson, who lived on a farm of his own and was prosperous, was warned by the whitecaps to leave, which warning he disregarded. About three or four weeks ago his home was visited in the night by whitecaps and several volleys fired into it. His wife was sick in bed at the time, with an infant only a few hours old. He still disregarded the warning, and remained on his place. Saturday he brought a young daughter to town in his buggy to spend the Christmas holidays with his brother, G. N. W. Wilson, of this city, and as he was returning home between sunset and dark was assassinated. Hilson is the second negro murdered by whitecaps in that portion of Lincoln county within the last month.

From all The Leader can gather of the facts and circumstances, it is a disgraceful state of affairs and calls loudly for determined action and corrective measures by law abiding citizens and all law officers of the county. An old farmer who lives several miles below where this murder occurred, stated while in The Leader office Monday, that about all the negroes had been frightened out of his neighborhood, and that all white farmers who had more lands than they could work themselves were left without labor and that these lands will have to lie out, uncultivated.

The Leader is informed that it is the intention of the British and American Mortgage Company, which has been an extensive loaner of money on farm lands in this county, to stop all further loans and instruct its agents and trustees to foreclose all mortgages that are not promptly satisfied before the situation grows worse and the lands become less valuable.

Our local banks share this same feeling of distrust and uneasiness, and will either be forced to refuse loans in localities where this disturbance of negro labor prevails, or else demand greater security and a higher rate of interest on such loans as are advanced.

The situation is indeed a serious one to the farmers and the financial interests of the entire county, to say nothing of considerations of humanity and our boasted Christian civilization; and these dastardly white cap outrages ought to be suppressed and those who commit them hunted down and brought to justice.

ONE TO MURDER IN HILSON CASE,

The Grand Jury Still Digging Up Violators of the Law.
After Saturday's Leader went to press the trial of Oscar Franklin for the murder of Eli Hilson in December, 1903, was set for today and a special venire drawn, and the trial of Will Franklin, charged with the murder of Henry List in November, 1903, was set for next Friday and a special venire drawn.

Ever since the preliminary trial of Oscar Franklin before Justice Daughtry, it has been known to those in possession of inside facts that the Franklins were weakening. Yesterday forenoon, while court was in session, Judge Wilkinson was notified by Mr. James Cassedy, attorney for the accused, that Oscar Franklin was willing to come into court and plead guilty to the Hilson murder and accept a life sentence, and that Will Franklin was willing to plead guilty to manslaughter in the List killing and accept whatever sentence the court might see fit to impose. District Attorney Webb and Mr. Brady, for the State, signified that this would be acceptable to them, and the prisoners were brought in and entered their pleas accordingly.

This sudden termination of these two important cases was a great surprise to the public generally and has been the chief topic of conversation since. The Police Think He Was the One that Fired the Shot-Burke Died at the Hospital.
The entire community around the Kingan packing establishment was aroused to a high pitch of excitement yesterday afternoon by the report of an attack made upon Gertrude Worth, the thirteen-year-old daughter of Mrs. Eva Worth, 613 West Maryland street, by Eugene Burke, a negro, who had been seen loafing around the vicinity for several days.

As a result Burke was later shot and killed by a man who is thought to be James Anderson, an employee of the Kingan Packing Company. The negro, it is said, forced his attentions on the child as she was gathering kindling wood around the platform of the packing plant and grabbed her by the arm, at the same time grossly insulting her. The girl cried out from terror and her screams attracted the attention of several men and boys who were in the neighborhood. A chase for the negro was begun at once. Up one street, down another and over the I., D. & W. railroad bridge went the fleeing negro with the angry mob howling close on his heels.

After crossing the bridge some of the pursuers turned and went back, but it is said that Anderson continued the chase for several blocks and on seeing that it was impossible to catch the man alive drew his revolver from his pocket and fired. At the same time the colored man had turned and, picking up a stone from the roadside, hurled it at Anderson.

SHOT WAS FATAL.

The shot from the revolver struck him in the abdomen and he fell in his tracks bleeding profusely, but was soon on his feet and continued his flight, rushing blindly over the embankment at the old circus grounds where he was later found in a dying condition. Dr. Sheek, of the City Dispensary, was called and took the wounded man to the City Hospital in the Dispensary ambulance, where he died an hour later.

Bicyclemen Morgan and Simon went at once to the home of Anderson, 1330 West Market street, but found that he had been there and gone several minutes before. Detectives Asch and Manning were assigned to the case and a search was instituted for the man who did the shooting. The Worth giri was able to give but little information as to who fired the fatal shot, but enough evidence was gathered to make it almost certain that Anderson is the man. He was traced through Haughville and it is thought he has left the city. The police think there will be no difficulty in finding him, however, as he was dressed in a soldier's coat and cap and has several peculiarities which will locate him wherever he goes.

Mob Went After Him for It and One of Them Shot Him Dead.
INDIANAPOLIS, June 9.—Eugene Burk, a negro employed in the English Hotel, was murdered this afternoon for a supposed insulting remark to a thirteen-year-old white girl named Gertrude Worth. Burk was seen to stop and talk to the girl, who turned away from him, but he appeared to force his attentions upon her. He was watched by the employees at Kingan's packing house, and when he started away they began pursuit, being joined on the way by idlers who were on the street.

Burk ran down the railroad tracks with a mob of 200 at his heels, but suddenly a young man with a revolver in his hand dashed ahead and overtook the feeling negro. Burk turned as his pursuer gained on him and just as he did so the young man fired and his victim fell and rolled down the railroad embankment, dying almost immediately. The murderer is believed to be a man named Anderson. He has not been arrested.

AFTER SHOOTING BURKE HE WENT TO ELIZABETHTOWN.
Barr Said He Had Not Learned to Shoot in the Army for Nothing- A Hearing To-Day.
City Detective Chauncy A. Manning returned to Indianapolis early this morning with Mede Barr, of Elizabethtown, who is wanted here on the charge of murdering Eugene Burke, colored, Tuesday morning near the Kingan packing plant. Burke, it is alleged, grossly insulted little Gertrude Worth, thirteen years old, and Barr claims the negro attempted to stab her with a knife. After the shooting Barr left Indianapolis and went to Elizabethtown, where his father lives, and was later located by Sheriff J. W. Phillips, of Bartholomew county, and lodged in jail at Columbus.

When asked last night at the police station if he had killed Eugene Burke, Barr said:

"Sure, I killed him, and if he hadn't whirled around two or three time after I shot him I'd a shot him again. I ought to have a gold medal for it instead of being locked up here. He went up to this little girl and said, 'Hello, babe,' grabbed hold of her and attempted to assault her. Some other fellows and myself heard what he said and started after him, but they weren't game and dropped out before we got across the railroad bridge. I called to him to stop, and he drew a revolver out of his pocket and fired at me. And then's when I pulled my gun and put a bullet in him.

INTENDED TO KILL HIM.

"I didn't learn shooting in the army for nothing, and I intended to kill him when I started after him. And if I was on a jury and a fellow like me was being tried for shooting an ornery nigger like he was I'd turn him free and make up a purse of $100 for him. I don't think people will blame me for it after they know all about the case."

"Why didn't you turn yourself over to the police instead of running away?" he was asked.

The trial of Meade Barr, who shot and killed Eugene Birch during the month of July last in the vicinity of Kingan & Co.'s plant for an attempted assault on little twelve-year-old Gertrude Worth, was begun in the Criminal Court yesterday morning.

A strong witness for the prosecution was little Gertrude Worth, upon whom the assault was attempted, who testified that she was sitting on a car bumper when Birch accosted her and attempted to take her into a box car. She screamed and this attracted Barr and his companions.

Southern Cities Driving Out the Loafers and Criminals.
NEW ORLEANS, June 26.—The movement started in several parts of the South to get rid of the disorderly negro element responsible for most of the recent crimes in this section is gaining strength, and it is likely to become general instead of spasmodic, as formerly, and unload a large number of negro gamblers, confidence men and other criminals on the North.

The towns in southern Mississippi are following the example of Ellisville and Laurel in this matter, and ordering out all negro criminals, tramps and dangerous characters. Cooper, in Delta county, has started the movement in Texas. The negro loafers, negro sneak thieves and petty criminals of that town have been taken out by the Regulars, whipped and ordered to leave town.

Taking advantage of the excitement caused by the whipping, the houses of some of the better class negroes were placarded with notices to leave. They complained to the authorities, and at a joint meeting held at the court house the whites pledged their support to all orderly negroes, the negroes on their part promising to do all in their power to keep down the lawless element and to report all violators of law among the negroes to the authorities.

Teamster Uses Revolver, Which Later Wounds Another Man.
Providence, R. I., April 18.—Edward Baxter, a striking coal teamster, was shot to-day by a nonunion driver, Frank Howland, who ran away after firing five times with a revolver. He was arrested. Two of the bullets hit Baxter in the head, but neither wound is regarded as serious. It was alleged that Howland's horses had been held up by Baxter. Howland threw away his revolver. frank-howland-providence-1903-04-18.A9:
HOWLAND FIRES INTO CROWD. One of the Striking Teamsters Was Slightly Wounded.
PROVIDENCE, R. I., April 18.—Frank Howland, a colored non-union coal teamster, this forenoon fired five shots into a crowd of men who had attacked him, and two bullets struck Edward Baxter, a striker, but only slight injury resulted. Howland and Nelson Peters, colored, were badly bruised by the storm of stones which was hurled at them, and the report of the revolver probably saved them from being mobbed. Howland threw away his revolver and fled, but he was captured by the police before noon.

William O'Neil, 23 years old, picked up the weapon and carried it into a saloon, where he showed it to the bystanders. With the revolver pointed at himself, O'Neil, thinking that all the cartridges had been fired, pulled the trigger, and a loud report followed. Considerable commotion was caused by the shooting and medical assistance was hastily summoned.

O'Neil was taken to the Rhode Island hospital, where it was found that the bullet entered above the hip, causing serious injury.

In the meantime Baxter was arrested and taken to a police station on charge of obstructing the property of the Eastern Coal company. The police surgeon found that one bullet grazed his head, and another struck near the abdomen. The wounds were dressed and he was placed in a cell.

The shooting is the outcome of the teamsters' strike. With the exception of about forty men, formerly employed by the Eastern Coal company, the strikers were taken back at the time of the settlement of the dispute, last Monday. The men engaged by the Eastern company to fill the strikers' places were retained and the union decided to direct its efforts against that concern until the non-union m newere discharged. A number of assaults have occurred this week, in which the drivers were stoned and beaten, and the loads of coal deposited in the streets.

The story of the shooting, as told by the police, is to the effect that Howland and Peters, while going to their work, were attacked by Baxter and others. The negroes were struck repeatedly with stones, and Howland, warning that he would shoot, aimed the pistol. The crowd scattered in confusion. Two arrests were made today of other strikers, who made attacks on teamsters, and fines were imposed in the district court. A squad of twenty officers has been sent to the coal yards, where provisional police headquarters has been established to suppress violence on the part of the strikers.

FOR WHITE CAPPING
SIX CITIZENS OF PIKE HAVE BEEN ARRESTED.
They Are Accused of Grave Offenses and Government Agents Are Actively at Work Gathering Testimony.
Six citizens of Pike County charged with whitecapping are to have preliminary hearings before United States Commissioner Tutwiler in Troy Friday and Assistant District Attorney Julius Sternfield of Montgomery will go to Troy to prosecute the cases.

The defendants are: Boss Riley, Robert Windham, Temps. Chesser, Fletcher Windham, John Windham and William Pittman, well known white farmers residing about twelve miles from Troy.

These men are accused of a grave offense. It is alleged that they have repeatedly served notice on negroes to leave the county; that they whipped five or six negroes severely; that they are members of an organized gang which burned two negro churches; shot a negro woman and her baby and fired a shot gun into the house of a negro.

The six men were arrested Tuesday by Deputy Marshal J. F. Green who took them to Troy where they were admitted to temporary bail of $500 each by Commissioner Tutwiler who set their cases for trial Friday.

Government agents have been actively engaged in securing evidence in the whitecapping cases. A number of letters said to have been written Pike County negroes are on file in the office of the United States District Attorney. These letters are crudely written and some of them are filled with profanity and vulgarity. All of them demand that the negroes leave the county. They are signed "Negro Skinners," "Negro Killers," or with initials. One letter bears a heart and dagger, crudely drawn.

It is said that when the United States grand jury meets in Montgomery in December a number of whitecapping cases will be drawn to its attention. At least six of these cases will come from Barbour County.

UNCLE SAM TAKING HAND IN AFFAIRS
SIX WHITE MEN ARE ARRESTED NEAR TROY, CHARGED WITH WHITECAPPING-MANY OUTRAGES ARE CHARGED.
Montgomery, October 28.—(Special.)—Uncle Sam has taken a hand in the alleged white capping in Pike county.

Last Monday six white men were arrested in Lindwood beat, twelve miles from Troy, on charges of white capping. They were taken before United States Commissioner Tutwiler and admitted to a temporary bond of $500 each to appear before the commissioner on Friday, October 30, for trial. The white men who were arrested were Boss Riley, Temps Chesser, Bill Pittman, Robert Windham, Fletcher Windham and John Windham.

The federal authorities have taken up the matter because it is thought the white capping is in violation of section 5508 of the Revised statute of the United States.

These cases are peculiarly interesting on account of the fact that it is said some of these defendants have been indulging in the severe whipping of negroes, burning negro churches, and shooting into their houses to compel them to flee the country.

One case of peculiar alleged viciousness was where a woman with her baby was shot as she fled from her home.
garfield-williams-1903-09-07.A4:
HELD TO GRAND JURY
ALLEGED WHITE CAPPERS ARE BOUND OVER.
Testimony Before United States Commissioner at Troy Shows Bad Condition of Affairs in Section of Pike County.
Troy, Oct. 31.—(Special.)—Yesterday evening at 2 o'clock, the cases of Boss Riley, Will Pitman, Tumps Chesser, Robert Windham, John Windham and Fletcher Windham, charged with whitecapping, were called for preliminary hearing before Commissioner Tutwiler in this city. Assistant District Attorney Sternfeld was present to prosecute the cases.

Beside the large crowd of spectators present, there were about twenty-five or thirty witnesses for the Government, and about a dozen for the defendants. On account of the large crowd present who were anxious to learn the particulars of the cases, the Circuit Court room in the Court House was procured in which to hold the trials.

Failing to get through with the hearings yesterday, the cases were resumed this morning.

According to the evidence of the Government witnesses, rather startling conditions exist in Cross Roads and Linwood beats, about twelve miles north of the city. Negro churches were burned, negroes whipped and notified to leave the country. The house of Joe Browning was shot into and the house of a negro woman, Mary Clements, was riddled with shot and she forced to flee from her home. While running away from her house with her baby in her arms, herself and baby were shot. The shot took effect in the back of the negro woman's head and her baby was struck by shot; neither one being very seriously wounded.

The principal witnesses for the Government were: James and S. A. Daniels, Green and Henry Tate, B. P. and J. P. Floyd, C. W. and J. H. Parish, E. Golff, Clint Turner and W. C. Griffin, white men, and quite a large number of negroes.

Several notes warning and threatening negroes were introduced in evidence:

Garfield Williams, a tenant of James Daniels, received the following notice:

"Sept. 7, 1903.

"Garfield Williams, we warn you to square up your business and get out from here at once. If you owe anybody anything, pay it up and get out. And you must go twenty-five miles from here inside of five days, or death will be your portion. We intend to kill you if you stay around over five days.

"The W. C. of I. and C."

At the bottom of this notice is drawn the picture of a dagger and a heart. This notice was placed on the doorsteps of Williams. This negro is reputed to be a good farm hand and inoffensive.

Joe Browning received a notice inclosed in a miniature coffin, telling him to leave.

The whole crew of hands at Williams's mill were notified to leave the country or be killed. A number of them did leave, as well as a number of others who did not receive notices, but were frightened by the notices the others received, and the mill had to shut down. These negroes, it is said by some of the best white people of that community, are quiet inoffensive negroes.

Will Sewell, a negro farm hand, was whipped one night in April of this year so severely that the blood ran from his wounds and he was unable to work for three weeks. It was in evidence that he was whipped as a medicine and tonic. He was tied and castigated with a wagon whip.

The negro churches burned were Dunn's Chapel and Antioch.

The defendants, with the exception of one, are all young men. The other notices received by the negroes are too obscene and profane for publication.

It is said that there has been an effort made to intimidate both white and negro witnesses for the Government, and every effort on the part of the Government will be made to apprehend the guilty parties and put an end to these practices.

The witnesses for the Government are re-subpoenaed so that they can receive the protection of the Government.

The best element of the people of this county are bitterly opposed to this character of crime, as it tends to cripple the farming as well as other interests.

After argument of counsel for the Government and defendants the court held all of the defendants except Robert Windham, who was discharged. Fletcher Windham was held to bail in the sum of $750, and the others in the sum of $500 each, to await the action of the Federal grand jury which convenes in Montgomery next December.

NEGRO STARTED TROUBLE
GORDON DONALDSON ABUSED PERSONS AT UNION STATION.
He Pushed a Woman Carrying a Baby to the Floor and then Drew a Revolver—Later Arrested.
For a time yesterday afternoon it seemed that a mob would take charge of an impudent negro at the Union Station and had it not been for the timely presence of Patrolmen Dolby and Hite, who placed the colored man under arrest, it is probable that he would have suffered violence at the hands of the infuriated persons who crowded around him and menaced his life.

Gordon Donaldson, the colored man, has been in the employ of the C., H. & D. Railroad as a special officer for some time, but yesterday he was sent for by an official of the road who has an office in the Union station in order that he might be given his discharge, as his duties had not been performed in exact accordance with the wishes of the railroad company. Arriving at the station, which was crowded with excursionists and their friends, he assumed an authoritative air and demanded that the crowd move on. He then made his way to the door of the station, shoving people right and left, and in order to enter the building pushed a woman who was holding a baby in her arms to one side with such force that she was thrown to the ground and would have probably been badly hurt had it not been for the presence of a gentleman, who caught her in his arms and broke her fall.

CROWD MADE THREATS.

In an instant the crowd of travelers became vindictive and threats of "lynch him" were heard from all sides, while the negro stood in the corner of the doorway and glared defiantly at the white people from a pair of vicious eyes. The crowd within two minutes changed into a howling mob and vengeance was demanded by the spectators of the negro's insolence.

At that point Donaldson drew a revolver from his pocket and, flourishing it above his head, said that he would kill the first man who dared to touch him. However, on the arrival of the police he went with them to the police station without a murmur.

The officials at the Union Station say that Donaldson was employed as a watchman or special officer in the C., H. & D. Railroad yards and had no business at the Union Station except to call for his discharge. They say that his services have been very unsatisfactory to the company in the past and claim that he was not at the Union Station vested with any authority as an officer. The police say that Donaldson merely wanted to make a scene and on account of having a star on the lapel of his coat attempted to browbeat the people in the station. He was charged at the police station, where he was locked up, with drawing deadly weapons, and will be given a hearing in the Police Court this morning.

Secretary Butler, of the State Board of Charities, says children are being confined in the jails of some counties of Indiana illegally. He is making an effort to have all county authorities understand the law upon this subject.

"The last Legislature passed an act prohibiting any child under fourteen years of age being confined in a jail, police station or any other kind of a lock-up," said Mr. Butler. "The Board of State Charities believes that generally this law is understood by the county sheriffs, town marshals and city police authorities. All should understand it. Provision can be made in some one of the numerous children's homes or with the Board of Guardians, where such exist, to care for these children. In other counties they may be cared for in the sheriff's residence or by some family in its own home.

Doubtless some of these were properly cared for as is contemplated, but some of them, it is known, were confined in jails illegally."

henry-liste-green-grove-1903-11-24.A2:

One Negro Killed and Others Threatened and Shot at.
The white caps have been operating again in the southwestern portion of Lincoln county. On last Saturday night they visited the home of Eli Hilson, about seven miles from Brookhaven, who had been previously warned to vacate, and, it is reported, literally riddled his house with bulets.

How the negro and his family escaped being killed seems almost a miracle, but none were hit. It is stated that when this night attack was made, Hilson's wife had a baby but a few hours old. On the following Thursday night (Nov. 24) the whitecappers visited the house of Henry Liste, a negro living in the Gum Grove Neighborhood, and literally riddled List and his house with bullets. He only lived a little while after the shooting.

List's house was visited about two weeks ago and shot into and he was warned to leave, but he decided not to do so. He had lived in the community about all his life, and, so far as we have been able to learn, bore a good reputation. He lived on a small farm of his own which he had purchased about a year ago from A. C. Seavey & Sons of this city, and on which he still owed some.

After last summer's campaign closed, it was repeatedly stated by those in a position to know, that the white cap organization had disbanded in this county, and that there would be no more of this kind of thing. Instead, however, it is assuming a graver and more aggravated form.

WHITECAPS' TERRORISM.
Lawlessness Starts Afresh in Lincoln County, Miss.—Negroes Persecuted.

NEW ORLEANS, Nov. 29.—Whitecapism in Lincoln county, Miss., which has revived during the last two weeks, has grown much worse and has resulted in the killing of Henry Lisle, a negro farmer of excellent reputation. Several Whitecaps were arrested last spring, and this and the energetic efforts of Gov. Longino, it was thought, had suppressed the evil, but it has started up worse than ever.

Certain negroes were ordered to leave the county, and failing to do so were visited at night by a large body of armed Whitecaps on horseback. The house of Eli Hilson was riddled with bullets, but no one was killed. That of Henry Lisle at Green Grove was next visited and Lisle was killed. The attack on Lisle's house was the second made by the Whitecappers, who visited it two weeks ago, ordered Lisle to leave and fired into the house. He refused to go, and the second visit resulted in his death.

Public sentiment in the county is strongly against the Whitecappers. Gov. Longino has promised to take action in the matter.

henry-liste-green-grove-1903-11-24.A10:
ELI HILSON ASSASSINATED.
Waylaid and Murdered In His Buggy, While On His Way Home From Brookhaven.
Brookhaven.

Eli Hilson, a negro living about eight miles from Brookhaven, was assassinated within about a quarter of a mile of his home Saturday evening, while on his way home from town alone in his buggy. The bullet which killed him entered the side of his head near the ear and came out at the mouth. Death seems to have been instantaneous. The horse went on home, and his owner was found dead in the buggy on his arrival.

Coroner Geo. Lambright, Jr., visited the scene of the murder Monday, impaneled a jury and held an inquest, the verdict being that the deceased came to his death by a gunshot wound at the hands of parties unknown.

Last winter Hilson, who lived on a farm of his own and was prosperous, was warned by the whitecaps to leave, which warning he disregarded. About three or four weeks ago his home was visited in the night by whitecaps and several volleys fired into it. His wife was sick in bed at the time, with an infant only a few hours old. He still disregarded the warning, and remained on his place. Saturday he brought a young daughter to town in his buggy to spend the Christmas holidays with his brother, G. N. W. Wilson, of this city, and as he was returning home between sunset and dark was assassinated. Hilson is the second negro murdered by whitecaps in that portion of Lincoln county within the last month.

From all The Leader can gather of the facts and circumstances, it is a disgraceful state of affairs and calls loudly for determined action and corrective measures by law abiding citizens and all law officers of the county. An old farmer who lives several miles below where this murder occurred, stated while in The Leader office Monday, that about all the negroes had been frightened out of his neighborhood, and that all white farmers who had more lands than they could work themselves were left without labor and that these lands will have to lie out, uncultivated.

The Leader is informed that it is the intention of the British and American Mortgage Company, which has been an extensive loaner of money on farm lands in this county, to stop all further loans and instruct its agents and trustees to foreclose all mortgages that are not promptly satisfied before the situation grows worse and the lands become less valuable.

Our local banks share this same feeling of distrust and uneasiness, and will either be forced to refuse loans in localities where this disturbance of negro labor prevails, or else demand greater security and a higher rate of interest on such loans as are advanced.

The situation is indeed a serious one to the farmers and the financial interests of the entire county, to say nothing of considerations of humanity and our boasted Christian civilization; and these dastardly white cap outrages ought to be suppressed and those who commit them hunted down and brought to justice.

henry-liste-green-grove-1903-11-24.A13:
WHITECAPS REAP WHIRLWIND.
The people of Franklin county, who have been engaging in the whitecapper outrages for the past year or so, are now reaping the fruits of their folly. A new farming season is at hand, and it is impossible to induce Negro laborers to go to that section for love or money. Fancy wages are being offered to induce Negro immigration to Franklin county, but without any degree of successful result. The consequence will be thousands of untitled acres in the county during the coming year and a long train of evils are following in the wake of the lawless conduct that has been carried on by white men under the gulse of enforcing law and order.

In Amite county and some sections of Lincoln the situation is equally as bad. The Negroes have steadily drifted out of the three counties, going to the cano fields of Louisiana, the rich plantations of the delta or the saw mills of south Mississippi, until today the three counties lack at least 80 per cent of the labor they need to properly till the soil and raise the usual crops.

Sanders also shot Sergeant Thomas Gilhooley and Policeman Joseph Russo, both of Inspector Kane's staff, and the men will probably die, Gilhooley being shot in the abdomen and breast and Russo in both lungs. jefferson-sanders-new-york-1903-05-02.A4:
OPENED FIRE ON HIS TORMENTORS Negro Waiter in Saloon Known as the "Black and Tan" Shot and Killed One Policeman and Wounded Two Others EYE WITNESSES SAY THE OFFICERS WERE TO BLAME Teased the Negro Until a Fight Started When They Seized Him and Pounded Him on the Head with the Butt Ends of Their Pistols
New York, May 2.—Policeman Ernest O. J. Peters was shot and killed tonight in a saloon known as the "Black and Tan" at 6th Avenue and 3rd Street, by Jefferson Sanders, a negro ex-convict. Sanders also shot Sergeant Thomas Gilhooley, and Policeman Joseph Russo, both of whom will probably die. They beat the negro with their pistol butts but he was not dangerously hurt. He was captured after the fight.

The policeman, according to many witnesses, passed the greater part of the night in the saloon in which Sanders is employed as a waiter. The police say he has served 18 years in Sing Sing.

According to witnesses the three policemen teased the negro until a fight started when they seized him and pounded him on the head with the butt ends of their pistols. Sanders broke away and drawing a pistol fired one shot which killed Peters. Another policeman ran in from the street and attempted to arrest the negro when he opened fire again hitting Gilhooley and Russo, both of whom staggered out of the door and fell on the sidewalk.

When his pistol was empty Sanders was clubbed into submission. Neither of the wounded men was able to give any explanation of the origin of the trouble.

The house surgeon of the hospital said tonight that Russo would live but that Sergeant Gilhooley was mortally wounded. Both men were shot twice, Russo through the chest and Gilhooley in the abdomen and breast. The doctor declared he found no traces of liquor on either man. He refused to permit the coroner to talk to them as he said they were not in condition to be spoken to. The coroner will try to get their ante-mortem statements tomorrow.

NEGRO'S VICTIMS TWO. POLICE SERGEANT DEAD.
Policeman Russo Unable to Tell How Trouble Began.
Surrounded by his family, but unconscious when the end came, Sergeant Thomas Gilhooley, one of the three policemen shot by the negro, Jefferson Sanders, in a fight at the Lenox Hotel, Sixth-ave, and Third-st., died at 7:20 o'clock last night in St. Vincent's Hospital. Policeman Ernest O. J. Peters was killed almost instantly. Policeman Joseph Russo is in St. Vincent's Hospital, with a bullet hole through his right lung and a serious scalp wound. One bullet is still in his body. His condition is serious, but he may live. By what the surgeons consider almost a miracle, a bullet which struck his head, was deflected by his skull.

The exact circumstances leading up to the affray were still unknown last night, contradictory stories having been told, and it being impossible to get an ante-mortem statement from Gilhooley. A statement was obtained from Russo, but it is of little value, as he said he did not see the beginning of the trouble. Sanders told his story at length in the Jefferson Market court prison, admitting that he shot, believing that his life was sought by the policemen, whose identity, he asserted, he did not know. He persisted that the three policemen deliberately raised a "muss." On the other hand, Coroner Scholer says he obtained a version from a good source that Sanders was urged to "do up" the policemen by an offer of a $20 bill.

Inspector Kane, of Queens, to whose staff the policemen belonged, said they had no reason to be in the resort where the fight started, or even in Manhattan.

Arraigned before Magistrate Pool in the Jefferson Market court yesterday, Sanders was held without bail to await the action of the Coroner. Five witnesses were committed to the House of Detention.

During the court proceedings, a crowd gathered about the patrol wagon in which Sanders and the witnesses had been taken to the entrance of the Jefferson Market prison. For a time it looked as if an attempt would be made to assault Sanders if he was taken from the court to the Tombs Prison. He was, however, placed in a cell on the top floor of the prison, where he made a statement. His head was wrapped in bandages, and his clothes, collar and shirt were dyed with the blood that had flowed from the wounds on his head and face. He is a little man, possibly five feet seven inches tall. He said he was born in Marion-st., this city, fifty years ago. His story in part was as follows:

After the men ordered their drinks the big man (Gilhooley) threw his beer on the floor. Then he said to the other two: "We'll have a muss with these coons before we leave."

I was "tipped off" to their intention, and I wanted to give them no opportunity. But I watched them and saw them getting ready. Then I thought to go out the side door and get a police-man. As I started to go through the passageway to the side door the light haired one (Peters) was standing in the way. I said, "Excuse me," and started to pass him.

"You black son —, where in the — are you going," he said.

"You haven't any cause to call me that," I said to him; "I am not offending you in any way."

He struck me in the mouth then, cutting my lip. I saw there was trouble coming, and I tried to avoid it. But he struck at me again, and the others came up and began to punch me with their fists—or, I should say, the big man with the mustache (Gilhooley). The little, dark man I don't think struck me at all.

I fought them off and ran out of the side entrance into the street, and up to the corner of Sixth-ave, where the front entrance of the saloon is, looking for a policeman, with the three men after me. Just as I got to the front entrance the men caught up to me, and, backing into the saloon, I did the best I could to defend myself.

New York, May 3.—Police Sergeant Gilhooley, who was shot last night by Jefferson Saunders, a negro waiter, who at the same time killed Policeman Peters and desperately wounded Policeman Russo, died in the hospital tonight. Russo's condition is dangerous, as he was shot through the lungs, but he has a fair chance of recovery. Saunders was held here today to await the action of the coroner.

He made a statement that he had been assaulted by the three policemen, who were unknown to him and were in citizens dress and that he used his pistol in self-defense. Six witnesses of the affair were committed to the house of detention. Saunders, according to the police has been known as a 'bad nigger' for many years. He has been concerned in numerous shooting and cutting affrays and has served in all nearly 20 years in Sing Sing.

AN EYE FOR AN EYE
A colord man down South hearing not long since of the lynching out West of one of the race, exclaimed, "Well it seems the Negro is surely in the whole Union now." An incident in New York city on Saturday night last gives point to the exclamation Three policemen, over from the "old country" probably for only a brief space—one of them was named Gilhooly—went into a saloon and after a vulgar carousal started a "rough house" with the patient and courteous waiter, Jefferson Saunders, who was there to make an honest living, and who had supplied them with all for which they called. Saunders bore their sneers and taunts in silence, reluctant to jeopardize his place and his power to support his family by active resentment. Mistaking his silence for poltroonry these guardians (?) of the law with the usual instincts of the coward proceeded to do him up physically, with the result that two of the assailants are dead and the life of the third is despaired of. Abraham Peters, cashier at the Lenox Hotel, said that after Gilhooly, Peters and Russia got into the fracas with Sanders, two of the men began beating the negro with the butts of their revolvers.

jefferson-sanders-new-york-1903-05-02.A25:
KILLED TO SAVE SELF.
Grand Jury Frees Negro Who Shot Two Policemen.
Jefferson Sanders, the colored man who on May 2 was beaten and then killed two policemen and shot another, was yesterday released from custody by Recorder Goff, in Part I of the Court of General Sessions.

On the day of the shooting the police parade took place. Sanders was employed in what was known as the Lenox Hotel, at Sixth-ave. and Third-st. At the close of the parade Sergeant Thomas Gilhooley and Patrolmen Ernest Peters and Joseph Russo, all members of Inspector Kane's staff in Long Island City, entered the hotel and created trouble. Sanders was badly beaten, and then, it is alleged, he pulled his own revolver and fired at the three men, killing Peters and Gilhooley and injuring Russo so severely that he remained in a hospital for some time. Sanders was also a patient in the hospital until a short time ago, when he had recovered sufficiently to be removed to the Tombs.

The Grand Jury yesterday spent two hours considering the evidence adduced in the case by the District Attorney's office, and failed to find an indictment. Assistant District Attorney Perkins said in court that from the evidence in the case it was clearly shown that Sanders had been attacked by Gilhooley, and that, according to what witnesses he had been able to secure, the colored man did not pull his revolver until he had been beaten by the policemen and they had drawn theirs. Russo, since the shooting, has been remanded to patrol duty.

Marshal of Mississippi Town Fails in Attempt to Save Life of a Negro Murderer
"JIM' CARR IS HANGED
Taken From Officer While Being Hurried Away at Night From Scene of His Crime
Special Dispatch to The Call.

NEW ORLEANS, Dec. 27. — "Jim" Carr, the negro who killed Deputy Marshal Cobb at Saucier, in Hancock County, Miss., yesterday, was lynched by a mob at Millview last night.

Carr was disturbing the peace. When the officer attempted to arrest him Carr shot Cobb, killing him instantly. The Marshal of Saucier returned the fire, wounding the negro, who was then locked up in the town jail.

An attempt was made to lynch him, but was prevented by the Marshal. As it was feared that the mob would return, the Marshal hurried the prisoner away in the night, intending to take him to the County Jail at McHenry, which is safe against attacks, but he was waylaid in the pine woods by the mob and the prisoner was taken from him and hanged.

LYNCHING DID NOT OCCUR IN TOWN OF LOWRYSVILLD.
Chester, May 2. There was great excitement here last night about 9 o'clock when it was reported that a lynching bee was imminent at Lowrysville, seyen miles north of this place. The report was greatly exaggerated, but to preserve Chester's reputation against all kinds of lawlessness Solicitor Henry asked Gov. Heyward for military assistance for Sheriff Cornwell. After a prompt reply from the governor the sheriff, accompanied by the Lee Light Infantry, 42 strong, left on a special train for Lowrysville. They did not find a large crowd as was expected and no demonstration whatever was made.

It seems that some time in the early morning Jim Montgomery, a burly young negro, went to the house of Mrs. Neely Smith, a highly respected and aged widow, presented a pistol and declared that if an alarm was made he would shoot. Mrs. Smith's grand-daughter, the only other occupant of the house, did not hear the threat, but ran and called neighbors and the intruder ran off.

The negro was tracked and caught about dark. He was locked up in a store and surrounded by armed men.

When the sheriff reached the scene he met with no resistance whatever in claiming his prisoner and the special train returned here at 12 o'clock. The negro was confined in jail and will be held for trial at the next term of court.

Jim Gilmore was captured at P
Jim Gilmore was captured at Pursley & Parrott's saw mill, near King's Mountain last Tuesday evening by Sheriff Logan and Messrs. Calvin Pursley and C. F. Gordon.

Gilmore is the negro who was arrested at Lowryville last year on the charge of having broken into a house occupied by some unprotected ladies. He had a narrow escape from being lynched at the time and after he was committed to the Chester jail, it was necessary to call out the military company to protect him from violence. He made his escape shortly afterward and nothing had been heard of him since.

Gilmore had been working at the saw mill since early spring; but it was only a few days ago that his identity with the man wanted in Chester became known to the whites. Mr. Calvin Pursley was the first man to make the discovery. He promptly notified Sheriff Logan and the raid of Tuesday night was planned at once.

"Feeling pretty sure," said Sheriff Logan in telling about the arrest, "that if we approached the fellow in daylight, he would run, and knowing the custom of the saw mill people I arranged to get there about supper time. The hands live in little shacks, without windows and only one door and when you come up to the door you need not let anybody get by you unless you want to.

"It turned out about as I expected. There were the negroes eating supper, and I began asking first about some lumber in which I pretended to be interested. Then I wanted to know whether any of my old saw mill niggers were still in the business, and asked about first one and then another until in this way we spotted Gilmore. He did not try to deny his identity, and we started on for Yorkville with him." Gilmore is about thirty years of age, ginger cake color and a fine physical specimen, just such a fellow as is wanted about a saw mill to do heavy lifting. Sheriff Cornwell came up from Chester Wednesday morning and took the prisoner back to Chester on the freight train.

RACE WAR IN THE BRONX
NEGRO CUTS WHITE MAN.
Rioting Ensues, and Many Persons Are Hurt.
In race rioting in The Bronx last night John Finnessy, forty years old, of No. 808 Jackson-ave., was stabbed in the abdomen, probably fatally, by a negro, who escaped. Fifty men with billiard cues and liquor bottles and a dozen detectives were chasing him at a late hour. The stabbing resulted in a race riot, and a hundred and fifty white men hunted negroes all night around the scene of the stabbing, at One-hundred-and-fifty-fifth-st. and Washington-ave., bruising and beating them and driving them into their homes or elsewhere, until the police became numerous enough to prevent further rioting. The reserves had to be turned out, as negroes and whites rushed to the scene to help their companions.

Two unidentified negroes did some drinking in the saloon of Gustave Kanze, at the southwest corner of One-hundred-and-fifty-fifth-st. and Washington-ave., about dusk last night, and had a quarrel with the proprietor about the payment of the last round. They settled, but were surly, and had to be put out. They threatened vengeance on the proprietor. They and a dozen other negroes were seen about 8:30 o'clock opposite the saloon. Allen Price, of No. 10 Weir Court, said he overheard threats to kill "Gus," who he believed to mean Karze. One of the negroes went to the saloon door and called to Kanze to come outside.

FIRST ACT OF VIOLENCE.

Kanze was busy and did not leave, but Finnessy went to the sidewalk. The man who had called went back to the other negroes, and a knife was seen passed around among them. The first man took it and went back to Finnessy. He attacked the white man, stabbed him twice in the left arm, and then gave him a vicious dig in the abdomen, causing a wound six inches wide and two inches deep. Finnessy fell unconscious on the sidewalk, where he was left for a time, while fighting and rioting raged all about and around him.

The men in the saloon felt that trouble was brewing when the negro called to Kanze to come out, and they seized billiard cues and glasses and bottles, and rushed to the street. The man who did the stabbing fled toward Jerome-ave., and a lot of the men went after him.

"Kill him! Kill that nigger! Stone him! Shoot him!" were some of the shouts that went up from the pursuing crowd.

RIOTING BREAKS LOOSE.

The dozen negroes who had accompanied Finnessy's assailant were attacked by the mob of men, aided by a lot of white laborers of that neighborhood, who fled out of their homes with all sorts of weapons. They rushed at the negroes, beat them with stones, sticks, billiard cues, glasses and bottles, cut a number of them and bruised all, and drove them into the darkness or to their homes.

All the time women and children were fleeing to their own or neighbors' homes, and whites and blacks were running out of their houses to help men of their own race. Many negroes live on One-hundred-and-sixty-fifth-st., near Washington-ave., and many of them ran out with knives and whatever they could use as weapons, the whites running out with similar weapons. None had revolvers, and no shots were fired, but this is believed to be caused by the fact that people about there are too poor to have pistols.

The neighborhood was in a state of terror. Yells of brutal vengeance, of triumph, of terror, of pain, of anger and of command came from one side and the other as whites and negroes clashed and beat each other. Policeman Belton, of the Morrisania station, ran up with a club, but no one paid any attention to him, and he ran to a telephone, calling on his station for aid and the Lebanon Hospital for an ambulance and surgeon for Finnessy. Half a dozen detectives ran down from Morrisania station, but they saw such a hopeless riot before them that the reserves were asked for immediately, and the wagonful of men was run down as fast as the horses could draw it.

MANY MEN HURT FIGHTING.

Dozens of white and colored men were cut in the fight. Many cut negroes, with faces bleeding, were seen running into their homes near by. After a little time, they found themselves so inferior in numbers that they retreated, and the white men, yelling triumphantly, fell on them bodily and bruised and cut them until all fled in terror.

Just as the last of the white men were returning from the chase four negroes, who knew nothing of the trouble, walked into Kanze's saloon. The white men rushed at the negroes, beating them with fists and clubs, and when they saw the police coming bolted the doors. The police broke in the door and rescued the colored men. They kept the white men off until they escorted the negroes out of sight.

Captain Byrne, of the Morrisania station, sent out a squad of men to capture the man who stabbed Finnessy and prevent any harm coming to him. Finnessy was taken from the sidewalk, where he lay bleeding during the rioting, and taken to the Lebanon Hospital. He was at once placed on the operating table, but his chances were regarded as slim.

Charles Jackson, alleged slayer of Charles Roxbury, the tea taster, is supposed to have belonged to the same crowd of negroes which assailed Finnessy.

HUNDREDS JOIN IN BRONX RACE RIOTS One Man Is Seriously Wounded in a General Fight with Negroes. ROW STARTS IN A SALOON Reserves Called Out and Neighborhood Is Searched in Vain for the Offenders.
There was every indication for a few minutes last night that a serious race riot would develop in the Bronx. As it was, one white man was so badly cut with a razor that he is not expected to live, and several negroes were saved from the vengeance of a crowd by the presence of the police reserves.

John Finnessy, of No. 808 Jackson avenue, who keeps a livery and boarding stable at 154th street and Washington avenue, was in the saloon of Gustave Kanze, at 155th street and Washington avenue, a few minutes before seven o'clock, when several negroes entered the place, and in doing so jostled Fennessy's arm so that the gltss he held in his hand was overturned.

A fight followed, and the proprietor taking Finnessy's part, the two succeeded, after a lively scrimmage, in putting the negroes into the street. But they had retreated merely to obtain reinforcements. Allen Price, who knows Kanze, heard their threats, hastened to give warning and joined Kanze and Finnessy in the saloon.

The trio armed themselves with billiard cues, and had waited for two hours, when a score of negroes appeared across the street from the saloon.

One of them crossed the street and, pushing open the swinging doors of the saloon, dared any of the white men within to put a foot outside. Finnessy rushed at the negro and hurled him to the ground, but an instant later uttered a scream of pain, as the man got to his feet and disappeared in the darkness, his companions scattering. The negro's razor had inflicted probably mortal wounds.

Attracted by the noises, nearly one hundred men soon started in pursuit. Policeman Belton, of the Morrissania station, sent in a call for the reserves. The fugitives/were not again seen.

Finnessy was taken to the Lebanon Hospital, where his wounds were pronounced serious, and at midnight it was said that he had but small chance of recovery. It was after the disturbance had in a measure subsided when four negroes, who must have been ignorant or what had taken place, entered the saloon and called for a drink. A dozen men set upon them. The negroes being roughly handled when the police came to their rescue, and, recognizing that they had had nothing to do with the original trouble, helped them to escape.

NEW ORLEANS, May 31.—Henry Johnson was hanged the "Nacogdoches way" at Kaufman, Tex., yesterday, for an assault on Mrs. Wentworth. He was hanged legally within four days of the crime. The case was so railroaded through the courts that there was no time to erect a gallows in the jail. It was impossible under these circumstances to enforce the State law, which forbids hanging in public, and thousands of persons came into Kaufman from the surrounding country and witnessed the hanging.

There was no attempt at violence. The militia, sent to Kaufman to prevent a lynching, were drawn up in the railroad yard and kept the crowd back until the body had been cut down.

The negro confessed that he committed the crime for which he paid the penalty. The law requires that a condemned man shall have thirty days of grace after the sentence of death has been pronounced, but the negro waived this and also waived any appeal to a higher court, as Mrs. Wentworth is lying at the point of death. Great difficulty was encountered in preventing a lynching and only the presence of militia stopped Judge Lynch.

The Nacogdoches way of immediately hanging after sentence of death seems popular in Texas, where it is said to prevent mobbing, rioting and lynching, and also to deter negroes from crime.
