MURDER NOTICE TO ROOSEVELT
NEGRO APPOINTEES TO BE KILLED IF HE KEEPS ON.
New Orleans "States," Democratic Organ, Says Colored Federal Officials Will Be Murdered. "Just as the Negro Appointees of Other Republican Presidents Have Been Put Out of the Way"
Appointees of Other Republican Presidents Have Been Put Out of the Way"

NEW ORLEANS, Jan. 5.—The New Orleans newspapers all comment in savage terms on the action of the President in closing the Indianola, Miss., post office because of the resignation of the colored postmistress. The strongest expressions are from the New Orleans States, the Democratic organ. That paper says:

"In discussing the Indianola post office incident we do not believe it to be wise for either the people of the South or their newspapers to mince words. President Roosevelt, in closing the post office at Indianola, has suspended the law for the deliberate purpose of offending and insulting the white people of the South, and, incidentally, to pander to the negro vote of the Northern pivotal States.

"He has assumed the role of a Czar for the sole purpose of cinching the Presidential nomination in 1904, and it is well that the South should proclaim its knowledge of his motives, and also to impress upon the mind of the country the fact that if President Roosevelt has made up his mind to outrage and insult people of the South by appointing and keeping in office obnoxious negroes, his negro appointees will be killed, just as the negro appointees of other Republican Presidents have been put out of the way.

"Some persons will say, no doubt, that these are intemperate and violent views, but we are confident that they will be indorsed by the majority of the people in the Southern States. It may be said also that if Mr. Roosevelt's negro appointees are killed or run out of the country, he will dragoon the South with Federal troops. In such an event we are confident that the fact will be quickly established that our people are fully as strenuous as their Knickerbocker President.

"The people of the South were dragooned during the 'Dark Days of Reconstruction' and the history of that period shows that they did some dragooning on their own account. It was effective then and it is well for the President to know that it will be still more effective now. If he desires, in order to serve his own political ends to raise 'a rough house' in the South, he can rest assured that the game will be made entirely interesting for him."

The States has undoubtedly a great many with it although few have expressed their views as frankly.

INDIANOLA, Miss., Jan. 5.—Mrs. Cox, the former postmistress, accompanied by her mulatto assistant, left to-night for Birmingham. She denied that any violence had been threatened, but affirmed that she would not accept the post office again under any circumstances. Her husband, Wayne Cox, a railway postal clerk, gave out a statement this afternoon, in which he says that the people here are his friends.

"Two prominent citizens came to me and advised that my wife resign," he said, "and I understand the race problem and thought it best for her to give up the office. She acted accordingly. We do not feel offended and hope it will be convenient for us to continue to live here in peace."

"There is no doubt of the general sentiment against the reign of a negro postmaster at Indianola. The only friction that transpired was over the adoption of a plan to gain her removal from the office. At the mass meetings held in the court house, the Mayor was made chairman. Everything is quiet and no trouble is anticipated, since it is an assured fact that there will be no negro postmaster here. One could not be secured if the President so desired."

Mrs. Cox was presented with a request signed by fifty-four citizens, bankers, lawyers and merchants. It reads:

"We, the undersigned citizens, hereby request that you tender your resignation as postmistress of the Indinola office to take effect Dec. 1."

The interpretation of this resolution is worrying the signers. The Federal Court is in session at Vicksburg, Miss., and the signers of the request have a lawyer on the ground. They do not want to appear as violators of the Government laws. For this reason the identity of the signers could not be obtained by the newspaper correspondents in Indianaola.

An independent post office was established at the county court house to-day. It is maintained by the citizens and business firms, who contribute $1 and $2 per month respectively for clerks and carriers. The postmaster at Greenville has been instructed to forward mail received there to Heathman. Others instruct their correspondents to address their mail to Heathman. Heathman is a small village on the Southern Railway four miles distant. The carrier from here makes two trips daily.

The first wagonload of papers and letters arrived here at noon and was greeted by an assemblage of citizens. Prior to this the banks and merchants had mail received at Greenville shipped here by express. The new office is humorously deigned as "the white post office," but no sign on the door associates it with the Government.

Three newspapers have been accumulating the products of their printing presses and are at a loss to know in what way they can reach their subscribers. Indianola newspapers may not be mailed at Heathman. The site of publication will be changed if the post office matter is not remedied within a few days.

Communications have been received here to-day from many towns and cities in Mississippi suggesting concerted action all over the State to thwart President Roosevelt in securing the influence of the delegates in the National Republican Convention. An attempt will be made to secure a strictly white delegation.

Indianola has a population of 1,500, two banks, electric lights and water works and probably thirty-five business houses, including a big factory.

RISE AGAINST NEGROES.
Southerners Demand Resignations of Officeholders.
[BY TELEGRAPH TO THE TRIBUNE.]

New-Orleans, Jan. 6.—The excitement over the closing of the post-office at Indianola, Miss., by President Roosevelt is spreading over the South and a general uprising against negro officeholders is threatened. Special dispatches received here show that white people living along the lines of the Alabama and Vicksburg, the Vicksburg, Shreveport and Pacific, the Louisville and Nashville, and the Southern Railway have demanded the immediate resignations of the negro postal clerks running on those roads. The Post-office Department is much worried over the situation. There are two hundred negro postal clerks on the Atlanta division of the Railway Mail Service alone, and these negro clerks are reported to be in a condition bordering on a panic. So far no violence has been reported, but the postal authorities fear trouble. The impression has gone out that President Roosevelt is trying to force negro federal officeholders on the Southern people; and the feeling in the interior is running high as a consequence.

The Washington correspondent of "The Picayune" telegraphs as follows concerning the developments at the National Capital:

The negro question in the South is no longer food for mere jest in official circles, but it is exciting a serious nightmare among all who have to partake of it. Postmaster General Payne has reason to agree with the Bard of Avon, who wisely declared that troubles come not as single spies, but in battalions; for instance, the trouble at Indianola, Miss., which still haunts his pillow. He has been advised that the white citizens of the Beauf River, La., have ordered Charles Jackson, a negro mail carrier, to give up his position, and that the white people residing along the Alabama and Vicksburg Railroad are seeking the immediate discharge of all negro postal clerks.

The protest from those living along the Alabama and Vicksburg Railroad against the employment of colored postal clerks will come under the supervision of Mr. Shellenberger, the Second Assistant Postmaster General, to whom, as yet, the facts have not been officially presented.

"The people of the South are objecting to negro postal clerks," said Mr. Shellenberger this afternoon. "Not a few of them are concerned. On the Atlanta division I think there are at least two hundred such clerks."

POLICE KEEP ANCRY CROWD FROM SLAYER Shooting in Front of Mount Vernon City Hall Followed by Attempt of Murderer to Kill Detective Who Pursued and Caught Him. "LYNCH HIM!" CRIED CROWD SURROUNDING PRISONER. Six Officers Escorted Him on Turbulent March to Station House—Shooting Prompted by Jealousy and Victim Had Been Warned by Assailant.
MOUNT VERNON, N. Y., July 13.—Perry Griffin, twenty-three years old, a negro coachman employed on Chester street, here, shot and killed Eli Brown, twenty-five years old, also colored, in front of the Mount Vernon City Hall late this afternoon.

Griffin also fired at a detective, but the bullet missed the mark and he was disarmed and placed under arrest.

While the slayer was being taken to the station house a crowd surrounded him crying: "Lynch him." The throng pressed about in a threatening manner, and six policemen had all they could do to get the prisoner to the station house.

Griffin told the police that Brown had been unduly attentive to his wife and although repeatedly warned to keep away paid no attention to the threats and continued his calls.

Shortly before 3 o'clock this afternoon, while crowds of people were entering and leaving the City Hall, Griffin met Brown coming across the street. Without a word Griffin whipped out his resolver and fired three shots at him.

The bullets all took effect in Brown's head. Brown cried out:

"Now, you have killed me!" and then fell dead.

Griffin started to run and was followed by Detective Eugene Fisher. Being overtaken by the officer, the murderer turned the revolver on him and fired, but the detective was too quick for him, Fisher striking the weapon with his hand and the bullet going wide of its mark.

The negro fought desperately, though, until overpowered, some of the people in the crowd that gathered helping Fisher. Griffin was dragged still resisting, to the City Hall, where he was held for a time.

Later, under guard of six policemen, he was led through the clamoring throng to the station-house, the crowd on several occasions growing so threatening that the police had to make a show of force.

Griffin and his victim were both quite well known in this city.

MURDERED BEFORE 500.
Negro Coachman Shoots Another Four Times in Mount Vernon.
An old feud between Ell Brown and Perry Griffin, two colored coachmen for wealthy residents of Mount Vernon, because Griffin said Brown paid too much attention to his wife, ended yesterday, when Griffin shot Brown dead in front of the Mount Vernon City Hall.

The murder occurred in plain sight of five hundred excursionists who were on Huckleberry trolley cars bound for Glen Island, and at one time it was feared that the murderer would be lynched. Griffin, who is locked up at Police Headquarters charged with murder, is employed by Dr. Ronaldson, while the dead man was coachman for Minot C. Kellogg, a bank president.

Griffin says that Brown threatened his life. "He pulled a stone from his pocket, and I thought he was going to hit me," said Griffin. "He was a bigger fellow than me, so I just let him have four bullets." The bullets struck Brown in the head, and as he fell dead he exclaimed "Now you have killed me!" Griffin started to run, but was followed and captured by Eugene Fisher, a former detective. Griffin tried to shoot the detective, the latter says, but the weapon was struck from his hand. Fisher dragged Griffin into the City Hall, where he turned him over to Patrolman Marz. It took six policemen to guard the prisoner, so furious against him was the crowd.

Coroner Weisendanger began the inquest last night, and heard a dozen witnesses. As to Griffin's assertion that Brown had a stone in his hand and threatened him, the witnesses agreed that Brown made no motion, and that while the men were quarrelling Brown did no overt act. It was shown that about half an hour prior to the shooting Griffin went to a hardware store and purchased the revolver. Witnesses of the shooting said that as the men were passing near the City Hall Griffin was calling Brown names, and that he suddenly drew the revolver and began firing. Both of the bullets fired took effect. Brown started to run and turned a corner, with Griffin following him. When both were fairly around the corner, it was declared, Griffin began firing again.

SIX IN "MURDERERS' ROW."
How Slayers Awaiting Trial in the White Plains Jail Pass the Time.
Not in a great many years have there been so many murderers in prison in Westchester County as are now awaiting trial in the White Plains Jail. District Attorney Young and his assistants are engaged in preparing the testimony for the trials, which will come before the Supreme Court and probably will last most of the winter. The cases, however, will be comparatively easy, because most of the six murderers have confessed, and there is strongly incriminating evidence against the others.

The occupants of "murderers' row" are Francisco Raffo, the Italian, who shot and killed Policeman Maurice Ahern, of New-Rochelle; Martin Ebelt, of Mount Vernon, who choked his wife to death with a shoestring and hid her body in a sewer; Pasqual Grieco, an Italian caretaker on the estate of Joseph Park, in Harrison, who quarrelled with Andrus Collandro, another caretaker, and shot him to death in Port Chester, last Sunday night; Oscar Borgstrom, of Mount Kisco, who cut his wife's head off with a carving knife; Perry Griffen, a colored man, who shot and killed Ell Brown, another negro, in front of the City Hall in Mount Vernon, and LeRoy Brown, also colored, of Peekskill, who killed Edward Thomas, colored.

The District Attorney will try Borgstrom first because he is a melancholy Swede and is likely to try to commit suicide. J. W. NEGRO DREW KNIFE
SOLDIERS AT GRIFFIN PROMPTLY ASSAILED HIM.
BY POLICE AND CITIZENS
THE MAN WAS RESCUED FROM THE INFURIATED SOLDIERS.
Serious Trouble Was Narrowly Averted—For a Time It Looked as Though There Would Be a Clash Between the Soldiers and Citizens Growing Out of a Difficulty Between the Negro and a Sergeant of the Second Regiment—This Is the Closing Day of the Camp.

Griffin, Ga., June 29.—But for the prompt work of a few cool heads there would have been a serious difficulty on Hill street this afternoon. Peter Stark, a negro, it is claimed, insulted a sergeant in the Second Regiment and was promptly struck over the head. The negro then drew a long knife, but instead of attacking the sergeant, backed out of the crowd.

When the negro was seen with a knife in his hand a large number of soldiers quickly ran to the aid of their comrade, and were about to do serious personal violence to the negro, when a few of the citizens of Griffin arrived, and with the police, rescued him from the infuriated soldiers.

The negro attempted to use the knife, but, fortunately, did not do so, and thereby saved his own life, for there is no doubt but that he would have been killed had he cut the sergeant.

The affair created intense excitement, and it looked for a while as if there would be a clash between soldiers and citizens. All parties were arrested, and tried before Mayor Bailey, who dismissed the cases, and the police escorted the negro to a place of safety.

Drilled Against Women.

One of the most interesting events of the encampment was the competitive drill given to-night, between a company composed of the most prominent young society women of Columbus and the Columbus Light Guards. The ladies were drilled by Capt. Illges and the Guards by Lieut. Woodruff. After the drill a german was given the young ladies at the Commercial Club.

Will Break Camp To-day.

The last dress parade of the encampment was given this afternoon, and the companies show marked improvement in formation and movement during the time they have been in camp.

The tour will end at noon to-morrow, and the men leave for their homes during the afternoon. No passes were issued to-night, and no one was permitted to leave camp after 7 o'clock. The result is that never on the last night of an encampment has the city been so quiet and orderly.

NEGRO DESPERADO SHOOTS AT OFFICER
North Birmingham the Scene of Exciting Chase
MISCREANT STILL AT LARGE
Officer Lark Strong Went to Arrest the Negro for Carrying Concealed Weapon and He Was Shot n at Twice.
Sam Bailey, a negro man who worked at the furnace at North Birmingham, caused intense excitement yesterday afternoon at that place and a lynching was only averted by his escaping from the mob who were after him. Officer Lark Strong went to arrest Bailey for carrying concealed weapons, who on the approach of the officer drew his pistol and fired, the shot coming close enough to tear the cuff off Strong's coat without injuring him.

Struggle Begins.

Before the negro had time to fire again the officer closed in on him and a terrible struggle took place.

During the scuffle the negro managed to get his gun in such a position as to use it as a club and succeeded in delivering a blow which sent the officer stunned into a ditch. Deputy Sheriff W. Coles arrived on the scene, and the negro beat a retreat into his house, evidently believing he had killed Strong. The officer, however, quickly recovered and with the deputy raised a crowd, who with pistols and shot guns advanced upon the house.

Makes His Escape.

The negro, evidently driven to desperation, fired several shots which were returned by the crowd. He managed to get out of the back door and fled, hotly pursued by the armed citizens who were determined to get him, dead or alive.

During the pursuit he fired two more shots at Officer Strong, two at a Mr. McCurry and also shot at L. Prost and J. Russell.

He kept up a running fire as long as he could get anything to shoot at, and his shots were returned, apparently without effect, although Marshal Cole stated last night that he was satisfied he was hit, as Mr. McCurrey used a shotgun.

Lost Sight of.

The negro was lost sight of at Baker's store at Jonesville, but the search was continued until dark. At a late hour last night Chief Cole said that the negro had been seen about dark in the neighborhood of Jonesville, and that he thought he would be apprehended. Mr. Strong was the only one injured in the affair. The blow delivered by the negro made an ugly wound on his right cheek bone.

For a Time the Shooting Was Promiscous, But the Black Succeeds in Making His Escape in the Woods.
Birmingham, Ala., Oct. 10.—While attempting to make an arrest in North Birmingham to-night, Deputy Sheriff Lark Strong was shot and wounded by Sam Bailey, a negro.

Unfavorable Conditions During the Past Week.
The mean temperature for the week ending 8 a. m. Monday, May 4th, was about 65 degrees, which is 3 degrees below normal. There were a few warm days during the middle of the week, but the first and last days were unseasonably cool, and unfavorable for the germination of planted seeds and the growth of young crops. The ground remains cold and owing to the lack of rain has become hard and crusted, this being especially true of bottom lands and clayey uplands. Frost occurred on the 28th at a few northern points, but did no perceptible damage.

There was a quite general rain on April 26th, accompanied by hail in the northern counties with a depth of six inches at Hickory. This rainfall was beneficial, but was followed by drying winds, and the need of rain is again noted over a large portion of the State, more especially in the truck raising districts. Shewers occurred over the central and eastern counties on May 3rd, the effects of which will be noted in next week's correspondence.

The dry weather enabled farmwork to make rapid progress and planting of the staple crops is nearly finished except that some upland and almost all bottom land corn remains to be planted over the western tier of counties, and bottom lands in the central counties, though some have already been planted in the latter.

Early corn is coming up generally and much has received its first working, but stands average only fair and are poor in localities, owing to the ravages of birds and worms, and to imperfect germination. Replanting is being done extensively. The weather has been too cool for favorable growth.

Cotton planting is nearly finished and will be entirely finished the coming week if the weather remains favorable, but owing to the prevailing coolness, germination is slow, and some seed failed to germinate at all. Many such fields are being replanted. Some fields have fair stands and are being cultivated, but the plants look sickly.

Tobacco is almost all transplanted, but is making no perceptible growth. Rice is in the same condition, with growth at a standstill. The Georgetown districts are being sown at this time.

In a few localities oats are promising and while still poor, show some improvement, but correspondents report the oats crop generally unpromising with probably half an average yield. They are heading low. Wheat is also poor, owing to rust and the hessian fly. Fruit continues promising, although pear trees are beginning to blight in various localities and peaches to drop in Charleston county. In the same county a green louse is damaging white potatoes. Rain and warmer weather would be of great benefit to all crops.

ALMOST A RACE RIOT.
Ruffians Assault Negroes—Rescue Prisoner, Beat Policeman.
Members of the gang of ruffians who hang around Seventh-ave. and Twenty-seventh-st. almost caused a race riot yesterday, and later severely beat a policeman who tried to defend an old man from the attacks of one of their number.

They had a rope and were throwing it out, tripping unsuspecting persons. When a negro, sixty-five or seventy years old, passed, they caught hold of the rope, formed a circle about him and danced, twisting his arms and legs tight and fast in the rope coils.

William Jackson, of No. 227 West Thirty-second-st., also a negro, tried to induce the gang to stop their persecution, and they turned on Jackson. He ran. The crowd chased him up Seventh-ave. to Thirtieth-st. They belabored him over the head and back with sticks, small stones and rope ends. Policemen Gilligan and Quinn, of the West Thirtieth-st. station, appeared, and with their night sticks beat back the crowd.

All the negroes along Seventh-ave. in that neighborhood had seen what was happening and had prepared to defend Jackson. They were swarming out into the street when the police rescued Jackson. Charles Staub, of No. 123 West Twenty-sixth-st., was arrested and charged with disorderly conduct.

An hour or so later Policeman Lane, of the Leonard-st. station, who was off duty, saw an aged man attacked by a young fellow in Twenty-sixth-st. near Seventh-ave. Lane, who was in plain clothes, arrested the ruffian and started toward the West Thirtieth-st. station with him. The prisoner suddenly turned on Lane and struck him in the ear. Lane had neither club nor revolver, and started to fight with his fists. Then there swarmed about the two men the Twenty-seventh-st. gang. They had the prisoner rescued in a minute and then attacked Lane. They knocked him down, rolled him over into the gutter, beat him and kicked him in the face and sides.

Policeman Doncourt rapped for aid, and when the police arrived, a minute later, the ruffans had fled, leaving Lane lying bleeding in the gutter.

BOYS START A LITTLE RACE WAR. Begin by Plaguing Passing Negroes and Wind Up by Chasing One.
Within half a block of the Tenderloin police station a dozen white boys started a small-sized race riot yesterday afternoon. The boys gathered at Seventh avenue and Thirtieth street. One of them had a long rope and every time a negro came along the boys would take hold of the rope and surround him. At first they were content to sing and dance around the victims, but after annoying a dozen or more men in this way they upset their last victim. He was an old man and William Jackson, a negro of 227 West Thirty-second street, went to his rescue.

The old man's tormenters turned on Jackson and their cries brought many other young rowdies. The crowd surrounded Jackson and began to strike and kick at him. Jackson fought back for a few minutes, but got frightened and started to run.

By the time he reached Thirty-first street there were fully fifty men and boys pursuing him. Yells of "lynch him" brought other loafers to the chase. At Thirty-second street Jackson ran into the arms of Detective Quinn of the Tenderloin station. Quinn drove the crowd back.

Jackson pointed out Charles Staub, 18 years old, of 153 West Twenty-sixth street as the ringleader of the crowd. Staub was locked up on a charge of disorderly conduct.
